B1.result: no verdict. The run's status is 'failed' and it carries no lab verdicts, so this branch rests on the arm-vs-control effects alone. Some cells kept only 8 or 9 of 10 blocks. Even so, the hypothesis that xs-rs still trails rsync on no-op re-syncs is refuted. At the default -j4, xs-rs against rsync was 0.269 (0.235 to 0.309, 10 blocks) on congress push and 0.308 (0.262 to 0.361, 10 blocks) on congress pull. It was 0.231 (0.219 to 0.245, 8 blocks) on psample push. The one weak cell is psample pull at -j4: 0.6 with a 95% interval of 0.213 to 1.689 over 9 blocks, too wide to call, at 45.418 s against 75.716 s. At -j8 xs-rs is clearly ahead in all four cells: 0.249, 0.268, 0.185, and 0.191 (0.147 to 0.249) on psample pull. -j1 is also ahead everywhere it is decided: 0.519, 0.584 and 0.421, with psample pull at 0.82 (0.317 to 2.121), inconclusive. Going from -j1 to -j8 roughly halves time on every cell, so no serial bottleneck dominates. xs-rs CPU seconds are close to rsync's at -j4 (7.747 vs 8.098 on congress push), not far above. The lab records only total CPU, not a user/kernel split, so branches 0 and 1 could not be told apart anyway, and neither is needed: xs-rs is at or ahead of rsync both ways. The remaining oddity is the high variance of psample pull at -j4 (and xs-cpp-j4 there at 2.002, 0.912 to 4.393). That is noise worth watching, not a deficit against rsync. A measurement changes no code, so keep is false.
